title: Remove a bathtub spout without a strap wrench
mechanism_check: Look underneath near the wall for a small hex set screw: present = slip-fit spout, absent = threaded spout.
Slip-fit slides over a copper stub and is held only by the set screw; threaded screws onto a pipe nipple.
improvised_tools: Small flathead screwdriver jammed diagonally into the hex set-screw socket (or a Torx driver tapped in gently).
Belt or rubber strap looped around the spout + stick through the loop = strap wrench.
Hair dryer heat to expand the spout and break the mineral bond; penetrating oil with 10 minutes to creep; hammer-handle taps around the base.
steps: Find the set screw first. If present: loosen it, then pull the spout straight off — never twist hard with the screw tight.
If threaded: heat the spout 2-3 minutes, apply penetrating oil, wait 10 minutes.
Wrap spout in a rag, cinch the belt strap-wrench, turn counterclockwise viewed head-on.
Brace the brass stub with your other hand so the in-wall pipe does not twist.
stop_conditions: The whole pipe starts rotating inside the wall — stop, you are about to cause a leak behind tile.
Chrome cracking or the spout body deforming under the strap.
Set screw stripped and spout won't budge: cut the spout off rather than wrench the stub.

title: Loosen a corroded outdoor hose bibb
mechanism_check: Confirm whether the bibb threads onto a pipe nipple or is soldered on — soldered means you must hold the pipe, not just the bibb.
Check if the handle stem or the whole body is what needs to move.
improvised_tools: Penetrating oil (or 50/50 ATF/acetone in a pinch) applied at the thread joint, 15+ minutes.
Two wrenches / pliers: one to turn, one to back up the pipe behind the joint.
Hair dryer or hot rag on the female fitting to expand it; cold on the male side.
steps: Soak the joint with penetrating oil; tap the fitting lightly to help it creep.
Heat the outer (female) fitting, then turn with a rag-wrapped grip while backing up the pipe.
Work it back and forth in small arcs — quarter-turn out, eighth back — to walk the threads free.
stop_conditions: The supply pipe behind the wall starts to flex or twist — stop and get a real backup wrench on it.
Fitting rounds off: stop before it becomes un-grippable.

title: Remove a stuck showerhead without scratching it
mechanism_check: Showerheads thread onto a shower arm; the arm threads into an elbow inside the wall — the arm must not rotate.
Mineral scale, not rust, is usually the bond.
improvised_tools: Rubber jar-gripper pad or rubber glove for grip without teeth marks.
White vinegar in a bag tied over the joint for 30 minutes to dissolve scale.
Belt strap-wrench for extra torque; rag to protect chrome.
steps: Soak the joint in vinegar to soften mineral scale.
Hold the shower arm steady with one rag-wrapped hand.
Grip the showerhead base (not the face) with the rubber pad and turn counterclockwise.
Re-wrap threads with PTFE tape on reinstall — 3 wraps clockwise viewed from the end.
stop_conditions: The shower arm moves in the wall — stop immediately; a broken arm inside the wall is a tile job.
Plastic showerhead body starts to crack: switch to hand pressure only.

title: Stop a running toilet with no parts on hand
mechanism_check: Lift the tank lid and watch: water running into the overflow tube = fill valve issue; water leaking past the flapper = flapper/chain issue.
Jiggle the handle: if running stops, the chain or flapper is hanging up.
improvised_tools: Hands only, plus a rag; a paperclip or twist-tie can re-link a broken chain.
A small weight (clean stone) can seat a warped flapper temporarily.
steps: Jiggle the handle to reseat the flapper.
If the chain is tangled or too tight, free it and leave 1/2 inch of slack.
If the flapper won't seal, press it down by hand to confirm, then weight it as a stopgap.
If water pours into the overflow, lower the float: bend the float arm down or slide the float clip lower.
stop_conditions: Tank components crumbling with age — forcing cracks the flush valve seat.
Water on the floor around the base: that's a wax-ring failure, not a tank fix — stop and shut the supply.

title: Unclog a sink drain without a plumber's snake
mechanism_check: Slow drain = partial clog near the trap (hair/soap); standing water = full blockage; gurgling = vent issue, not a clog you can reach.
Pop-up stoppers collect hair — pull it before anything else.
improvised_tools: A wire coat hanger straightened with a small hook bent in the end.
A plunger (flat cup for sinks); petroleum jelly on the rim improves the seal.
Baking soda + vinegar + a kettle of near-boiling water for grease/soap sludge.
steps: Remove the pop-up stopper and pull out visible hair with the hooked hanger.
Plug the overflow with a wet rag, then plunge 10-15 vigorous strokes.
For grease: half cup baking soda, half cup vinegar, wait 15 min, flush with hot water.
If the trap is accessible, place a bucket and unscrew it by hand to clear it directly.
stop_conditions: Multiple fixtures backing up at once = main-line blockage; plunging one fixture pushes sewage out another — stop and call a pro.
Chemical drain cleaner was already used: wear gloves/eye protection and do not plunge (splash-back burns).

title: Clean a mineral-clogged faucet aerator
mechanism_check: Weak, splaying, or uneven stream with good pressure elsewhere = clogged aerator screen, not a supply problem.
Aerators unscrew counterclockwise viewed from below; some need the little plastic key.
improvised_tools: Rubber glove or jar gripper to unscrew the aerator by hand.
White vinegar soak (30 min) to dissolve scale; an old toothbrush to scrub the screen.
A coin edge or butter knife in the aerator's notches if it has no grip.
steps: Unscrew the aerator by hand with the rubber grip.
Note the order of screen, mixer, and washer as parts come out.
Soak parts in vinegar 30 minutes, scrub, rinse.
Reassemble in the same order and thread back on hand-tight.
stop_conditions: Aerator housing cracks: replace the whole aerator (standard threads, cheap part).
No aerator and still weak: the clog is upstream — check the supply stops.

title: Stop a leak at a sink P-trap slip joint
mechanism_check: Slip-joint traps seal with a tapered washer compressed by a hand-tight nut — leaks mean a loose nut, a misaligned washer, or a cracked nut.
Drip only when water runs = joint leak; constant drip = supply-side, different fix.
improvised_tools: Hands first — slip nuts are designed for hand-tightening.
Rag-wrapped channel locks for a final eighth-turn; a spare tapered washer if you have one.
steps: Place a bucket, dry the joint, run water to confirm which joint drips.
Hand-tighten the slip nut; if it was loose, this usually ends it.
If it still drips, loosen the nut, check the tapered washer seats with the taper facing the right way, reseat, retighten.
Give it one careful eighth-turn past hand-tight with rag-wrapped pliers — no more.
stop_conditions: Nut is cracked or cross-threaded: tightening harder splits it — replace the nut/washer.
Trap arm misaligned so the joint can't seat square: loosen neighboring joints, align, retighten all.

title: Remove a stuck drain cleanout plug
mechanism_check: Cleanout plugs are large square/hex plugs threaded into the drain line; old ones corrode in place.
Cast-iron or brass plugs in cast-iron fittings are the stubborn ones.
improvised_tools: Penetrating oil soaked into the threads, 30+ minutes, reapplied twice.
An adjustable wrench on the square head; a cheater pipe over the handle for leverage.
Hammer taps on the plug flats to shock corrosion (not on the fitting).
steps: Soak threads with penetrating oil; tap the plug flats between applications.
Fit the wrench squarely on the plug head — full contact, no rounding.
Apply steady pressure counterclockwise; work back-and-forth in small arcs.
Once it cracks loose, unscrew slowly and have a bucket ready.
stop_conditions: The fitting or pipe starts to move with the plug — stop; you'll crack the hub.
Plug head rounding off: stop before it's smooth. A rounded plug needs a pro with heat.

title: Free a seized toilet/sink angle-stop valve
mechanism_check: Angle stops seize from mineral buildup on the stem; the packing nut around the stem is what you can safely work.
Know where the main house shutoff is before touching a stop that feeds a fixture.
improvised_tools: Penetrating oil on the stem threads; vinegar on visible mineral crust.
Two pliers/wrenches: one on the valve body (backup), one on the handle/stem.
steps: Locate the main shutoff first — a stop that breaks open needs it.
Soak the stem and packing nut with penetrating oil, 15 minutes.
Back up the valve body, then work the handle gently back and forth — never force a full turn from dead seized.
Once moving, cycle it fully open and closed twice to clear the seat.
stop_conditions: Valve body twisting on the supply pipe — stop, you're about to snap the stub-out.
Stem snaps or packing leaks steadily: shut the main and replace the stop.

title: Quiet water hammer banging in pipes
mechanism_check: Single loud bang when a valve shuts fast (washer, dishwasher, toilet) = water hammer; continuous rattling = loose pipe straps, different fix.
Old air chambers (capped vertical pipe stubs) waterlog over time and stop working.
improvised_tools: No tools: draining the system recharges air chambers.
Foam pipe insulation or rags to test whether straps are the rattle.
steps: Shut the main water off and open the highest and lowest faucets to drain the system.
Let it drain fully, then close faucets and turn the main back on slowly.
Air chambers refill with air and the bang should be gone.
If banging persists on one fast-closing valve, that valve wants a screw-on arrestor.
stop_conditions: Bang accompanied by a pressure spike or leaking joints: check house pressure (over ~80 psi needs a regulator) — not a DIY tune.
Rattling that draining doesn't fix = loose straps; secure pipes, don't keep draining.

title: Remove a tub drain without a drain key
mechanism_check: Tub drains thread into a drain shoe below; crossbars inside the drain are what a drain key grips.
Old brass drains corrode into the shoe — the shoe must not rotate.
improvised_tools: Two large screwdrivers or dowels crossed through the drain crossbars as a turning bar.
Penetrating oil around the drain rim threads, 20 minutes.
A rag packed below to catch the drain so it doesn't fall into the shoe.
steps: Dig out old plumber's putty around the rim and soak the threads with penetrating oil.
Cross two screwdrivers through the crossbars to form an X handle.
Turn counterclockwise with steady pressure, keeping the bar level so crossbars don't snap.
Lift the drain out; clean the shoe threads before the new drain goes in with fresh putty.
stop_conditions: Crossbars snap off: stop — the remaining ring needs a pro extraction tool.
The drain shoe rotates below: stop, you'll break the overflow linkage seal.

title: Temporarily patch a pinhole leak in copper pipe
mechanism_check: Pinhole = tiny jet or weep on copper, usually from internal pitting; the pipe wall around it is thin.
This is a stopgap — the pipe needs a section replaced. Shut the main if the jet is strong.
improvised_tools: A hose clamp (or two) + a patch of rubber (inner tube, rubber glove layers).
Epoxy putty stick as a second layer over the clamp if you have it.
Rag and bucket; know the main shutoff location.
steps: Shut the water off and dry the pipe.
Center the rubber patch over the pinhole, clamp it firmly — one clamp each side of the hole if the pipe allows.
Turn water back on slowly and watch the patch for 10 minutes.
Mark the spot and plan a proper pipe-section replacement soon.
stop_conditions: Pipe wall is soft, flaking, or green-crusted over a wide area: the pipe is failing, not the pinhole — patching invites a burst.
Leak is at a joint or the patch weeps under pressure: shut the main and replace the section.

title: Improve weak shower pressure: find the restriction
mechanism_check: Weak at one fixture with good pressure elsewhere = local restriction, not a supply problem.
Suspects in order: clogged showerhead/aerator, flow restrictor, partially closed stop valve, kinked supply line.
Test by removing the showerhead: strong flow from the bare arm = the head is the restriction.
improvised_tools: Vinegar soak for the showerhead; an old toothbrush for the screen.
Adjustable wrench (rag-wrapped) for the showerhead; PTFE tape for reinstall.
steps: Unscrew the showerhead and run the bare arm — note the flow.
Soak the head in vinegar 1 hour, scrub the inlet screen, rinse.
Check the shutoff/stop valves feeding the shower are fully open.
Reinstall with fresh PTFE tape; if flow is still weak, the restrictor or valve cartridge is next.
stop_conditions: Weak flow from the bare arm too: the restriction is in the valve or supply — that's deeper work.
Old galvanized supply pipes: internal corrosion is the restriction — no cleaning fixes it; plan repiping.
